title: Pananpe Escapes from Demon’s Hands
text:
I am a rich man, richer than anyone else.
When I go to the mountains, I capture lots of deer and bears.
I also go down to the seashore to fish.
I’ve hauled in lots of things from the ocean and I’ve caught many things in the mountains.
One day, when I was down on the beach fishing, there was a demon up on one of the rocks.
The demon was fishing. [He said,] “I’ve found some delicious young meat.”
While saying this, the demon came toward me.
Since it wasn’t possible to escape, I stood still, he caught me, and put me in his boat.
Carrying me in his boat, we came to a cavern and as we went in to the cavern, there was a little demon there.
“My little demon, I’ve found some fresh, young meat. Make him eat a lot and when he’s fat, you will feel well fed if you eat him then. I wanted to find some young meat like this somewhere, but it was difficult to find.”
While he was saying this, [I stayed quiet,] unable to even be afraid, I stayed quiet.
Then, the little demon cooked dinner.
He fed me and the food was really good. While we were eating, the demon went to the mountain.
“Little demon, what sort of magic does your father practice?” I asked.
“Father practices magic, he practices magic with a ball of black string and a ball of white string,” he said.
“How does he do it?” I asked.
“If one throws the ball of black string forward the area in front of him becomes dark. If one throws the ball of white string backward, the area behind him becomes light. So, when one is escaping, if he throws the ball made of white string in front, and throws a ball made of black string backward, no one can overtake him, Father said,” he said.
So, “Won’t you get them out and show them to me?” I asked.
“If I get them out, Father would be angry, so I won’t do it,” he replied.
“It’s OK just to show me,” I said, and he did get the ball of string out.
“This is how he does it,” he said.
So, “What other sorts of magic does your father practice?” I asked.
“Father practices magic with a thin needle and a thick needle,” he said.
“How does he use them?” I asked.
“If one moves the thin needle toward himself, then he dies. If one pulls the thick needle toward himself, then he will come back to life,” he said.
“Won’t you get them out and show me?” I asked.
He didn’t like it [when I asked], but I asked him over and over and over with a smile on my face.
“I won’t escape anywhere. If only you would show them to me. I just want to see them because I’m bored,” I said.
Then, the little demon did bring them out and show me.
“One uses them this way and that way,” he said.
“Please put them in my hand so I can see them,” I said.
context: An Ainu folktale where a man uses his cleverness to escape from the hands of a dangerous demon.

title: The Singing Cuckoo and The Thunder God
text: A singing cuckoo, one of the eloquent kind, perched on the altar with inaw-prayer sticks. It was hopping from a seat on the right to a seat on the left. In the daytime for six days, in the nighttime for six days [the cuckoo] was singing and singing, and finally returned [to the sky]. SOME PLACE, [THIS IS A ] kamuy yukar, AT SOME PLACE, Why was I a person living as a lonely woman, I didn’t know that. However I was a lonely woman, then a young man came there [along]. I thought he surely was not a human, but a God. I realized that he was a God. The young man, whom I saw, came and had a rest at my place, so He ate and stayed for the night at my place and [so] we lived. Finally, we slept together. The singing cuckoo, one of the eloquent kind, descended. For six days, all day and all night only when [the cuckoo] was singing and singing, my husband didn’t eat, he was only lying in bed. I prepared a tray [with food]. As [my husband] didn’t eat any food, I was distressed by that. It was [so], but my husband wouldn’t get up, he stayed in bed. When the cuckoo flew away, [my husband] got up for the first time and came [out]. He took fire-chopsticks and sat down at the seat of honor. He shifted the coals from the shore [the edge of the hearth] to the sea [the middle of the hearth]. He shifted the coals from the sea [the middle of the hearth] to the shore [the edge of the hearth]. “My wife, if I speak, you should listen well. I am not a human, I am one of six brothers, the Gods of Thunder. All of my elder brothers have wives, but as for me, when I looked for a person who would be a good match for me everywhere in the place of Gods, I couldn’t find one, so I looked in the place of humans. There was no one suitable for me other than you. So I descended [from heaven] and we married. However since all the Gods said, ‘If you don’t return now, you won’t be able to mix with the Gods.’ [The cuckoo] argued with me. Because it was a cuckoo, who was sent down [by the Gods], it argued with me, so I’ll return and help my brothers. When six years pass, I’ll come and see you. If you make six hoods and put them on [your] head, and take one hood off a year, if you keep taking off one hood [every year], I’ll come and see you when six years pass.” Said my husband. Then he got up and through the window, under the window as if shaking off the dust, he rose up. Then my husband became a bird and jumped out to the outside altar with inaw, so I also rushed outside and looked around. Just at that moment my husband was flying up [into the sky]. My husband was dropping his tears like a summer rain. He kept rising and I was crying and crying. “My husband, it seemed that you were saying something.” I thought so and went in. I made the hoods and put them on my head. Then when one year had passed, I took off one hood, I kept taking off [the hoods]. When six years had passed, indeed my husband came to see me. I followed him along with me and went to heaven. In heaven the real marriage, the true marriage took place. There was nothing we had to worry about. When we went to heaven, there was nothing to complain about. It was a real marriage, a true marriage and we lived happily with each other.
context: An Ainu supernatural story about a woman who marries a Thunder God, waits six years for him, and eventually joins him in heaven.

title: The Girl in the Snow
text: I had a mother and a father, and we lived together. My father was a wealthy man, with no peers. He was a master of hunting, with no equals. Without wanting for food or things, I grew up. From then on, I made sure my father did not go to the mountains. I went to the mountains by myself and caught many deer and bears, but I wanted to go to the hunting cabin. I went to the hunting cabin and put up prayer sticks. When I went hunting, I went to the mountains when the weather was good. But the clouds gathered, and it started to snow. I did not know where I should go. As I was heading somewhere, I got caught on something and stumbled. When I dug it up, I found a very beautiful girl buried in the snow. She appeared to already be dead. I was not sure where I was, but I wrapped the girl in a straw mat and lifted her onto my shoulders. As I was walking aimlessly, the snow started falling. The snow was deep, and as I wandered around, I fell from somewhere and was surprised. I fell while still holding the girl. I had fallen through the skylight of the hunting cabin, falling near the head of the hearth. A handsome youngster was making an arrow. He was very surprised that I had fallen into the hunting cabin. We greeted each other, and the youngster took pity on me. “A bear's hide, anything. If you could lend me something, I can save this girl. I found her in the snow, but I can save her life,” I said. The youngster took heart and lent me a bear hide. I removed the girl's kimono, wrapped myself with her in the hide, and held her. The youngster was worried about us. “Start a fire. Make a stronger fire. Somehow I will revive this girl,” I said as I held her. I held her with my skin right against hers, and soon she started breathing. She had revived and started breathing, so I stood up and sat near the fire. When I glanced up, a large bear was standing at the skylight from which we had fallen. It had chewed charcoal rubbed on half of its body, with the drippings from salmon roe on the other. I had a quick look. I was angry, but without showing my anger, I called over the youngster who was making the arrows. “If you need a spear, make a handle for a spear,” I said. I took my mountain knife out of its sheath, and the youngster watched as I made a handle and burned it. He stood up, took a spear, and made a handle. He put the end into the flames. I looked up many times, and after a while, the bear fell through the skylight and landed on the seat of honor. I aimed for its large mouth and struck my spear through it. The youngster did the same, and together we swore and got rid of the bear. “Why do you do this?” we asked, swearing at it. The snow was deep in Iskar, so we dragged the bear toward the door and laid it down. Then I told the youngster what to do with the girl. “If you have something to make a porridge, anything, please give it to me. Then I will make porridge and feed it to her, and give her warm water to drink,” I said. He gave me a little refined grain, so I made porridge myself, cooled it off, and put it in the girl's mouth. She appeared to be feeling better, and in time morning broke. She warmed up, so I dressed her. I had held her with my skin against hers, and she came to. The girl had a change of clothes, but her clothes were frozen. I found some nice clothes in a straw bag, so I put them on her. When she got up, she faced the youngster and hugged him, saying, “Older brother!” The youngster also hugged her, saying, “Younger sister!” They both cried and held each other. “Did a young wealthy man from somewhere find my sister freezing to death?” he asked. “She regained consciousness,” I said. The youngster bowed to me many times. That night, I had a dream. A large man with a long red beard, long enough to cover his chest, appeared. He was almost as large as two people tied together and carried a large mountain knife. He spoke in an angry voice. “Young wealthy man from upstream Iskar, listen carefully to what I have to say. I am the god of storms and the god of snow. I am called the demon from the end of the mountains, but it is not that I truly had a bad spirit. Hear me, God of storms, God of snow. This girl from upstream Yupet River is such a beautiful girl in body and spirit. I said, ‘If the God of storms helps me, I want to kill her and make her my wife,’ and I asked for a snowstorm. I made sure that no one would want to walk in the storm and made the girl walk. When she came here, I was going to kill her and eat her, and take her spirit out. But you got there before I did. You took her and revived her. I was already broken and dead, so even if you throw me into hell as a bad god, you will not gain anything from it. So if you could make one small request, if you could ask that I become part of the Kamui, I will protect you, and you will have nothing to fear. You are also a descendant of a Kamui, and that girl is also a descendant of a Kamui. I have heard that you will become husband and wife. You must have found that girl with the help of the Kamui and revived her.” I saw this dream. I prayed and, even though I was angry, I sent the soul on its way. He had said that a small prayer would be enough, but I saw another dream after I sent the bear's spirit away more carefully than usual. A person who appeared to be a Kamui, with neatly cut hair, laughed and said: “What have you done? I said that you did not have to do it properly, but the prayers you said were so wonderful that now I am the chief of the Kamui. I am living comfortably, so I will make you rich as well.” I saw in my dreams: “Even though I had a bad soul, I never ate anything such as humans. The snow is deep, and there is nothing to eat. Even if you eat my meat, nothing bad will happen because of it.” Again, in my dream, the bear said: “If you sell my hide with my gallbladder, that money will make you wealthy.” The following day, the elder and I butchered the bear, cooked and ate its meat. I made the gallbladder and hide ready to be carried on the back and dragged them. Then the girl went into the house. Crying, she went into the house, and so did her brother. I returned to the hunting cabin. The weather had cleared up, so I returned to hunting. I caught many deer and bears, and then closed the hunting cabin. I carried that bear's hide, closed down the hunting cabin, and left my luggage of bear meat. The bear was large, so even the hide of its head weighed a lot. I carried it back to the village. Father said, “Son, why did you go to the mountain when the snow was so heavy?” “Son, I worried about you,” Father said. “For this and this reason, it is not like I had a very frightening experience, but I had an awful time. I returned to the hunting cabin and caught deer and bears, but I could not carry all of it back. Just this gallbladder and hide. I thought I would bring back the hide of the mountain's beast, and carried it back,” I said. Father rejoiced and held a ceremony to thank my safe return. I spent time without going to the mountains. One day, we heard a voice outside. When Mother went out to look, she said, “Two youngsters and one young girl. They have large bags.” So I told her to let them inside. The youngsters were brothers. “Older brother was hunting at the hunting grounds in Yupet. I am the younger brother. I do not know why, but we came to Iskar to hunt, and were building a hunting cabin,” said the youngster from the house where I had stayed. When I told them to enter, the youngsters came in, the older one first. The younger one followed him. Finally, the young girl came in. They sat down, so I greeted them, and then Father greeted them. “Your younger sister was able to live because of this young elder. Your younger sister has said, ‘I do not know how I was revived, but he is the only one I can marry.’ Because the youngster had told us where he lived, we came,” she said. Father greeted them again and again. I also did. The youngsters stayed at my house for many days and then left. They left the girl and went home. When the snow stopped, we traveled around. I had heard that their home was close by, so I took my wife. I was told that they were the elders of upstream Yupet, so we went to upstream Yupet. He said he was the village chief, so we went in front of the house. My wife dashed into the house right away. “I have brought the youngster who revived me,” she told her father. They were very pleased by that. The master of the house was a silver-tongued man. He greeted us. When the youngsters came home, they said: “Your younger sister survived because of our young lord. We should have gone to visit our younger sister, but before we could go, our young lord came to see us. Thanks to the Kamui, and thanks to the youngster who was really like a Kamui, we are able to live and see our younger sister.” We stayed for several days. Neither of them had wives, so they each took a beautiful woman as a wife. The older youngster began to live with his father, while the younger youngster built a separate house. They split their father's assets equally. We watched them live next to each other, and then left. After that, we lived at our home, and I went to the mountains where I caught many deer and bears. That girl was a hard worker. As we continued our lives, soon she became pregnant and gave birth. A boy was born. “Just as we were hoping for a cute child, son's wife was blessed with a boy,” my mother and everyone said in joy. We continued with our lives. We did not want for food or things, but I was afraid that a bad bear might appear. When I wanted to go to upstream Yupet, I went by myself, or I carried our child on my back and went to Yupet together with my wife. The older brothers at Yupet treated me as a brother and came to visit us. In time, our parents grew old. I continued my life without fearing anything and without wanting anything.
context: An Ainu folktale about a hunter who rescues a girl found in deep snow, encounters a powerful bear and receives guidance from Kamuy spirits.

title: White and Black Clew
text: There was my mother and my younger brother, and the three of us lived together. Once, when our mother was going out, she said, “I must tell you about your uncle. He may bring some food. But while I am away, don't eat it!” After saying so, she went out. We stayed at home and, indeed, an old man came. Holding a single deer foreleg in his hands, he came in. “Please eat it! Oh, you have grown so big indeed! You are so big, you can already start working! Let's go to work tomorrow! I'll come and meet you.” Saying so, our uncle went away. Our mother came back, and I told her what had happened. “He is at it again!” she said. “Saying the same things, your uncle also took your father away with him and left. It is a fact that your father never came back. And now again your uncle said that!” While saying so, our mother became angry. Although he had said “tomorrow,” I thought tomorrow meant when it became light outside. Before the day had broken, while it was still dark, our uncle came. “Hi! I came to meet you.” As he said that, I got dressed. Then my mother brought me one white clew and one black clew. “If you get scared of anything, throw the black clew to that place, and throw the white clew behind you.” Saying so, my mother gave me the two clews. I put them in my bosom and went. I was taken aboard my uncle's boat. We went, and finally the day broke. I looked around and, oh, there were so many frightening things, things that people are usually afraid of. “Here is the usual place we work at.” Saying so, my uncle moored the boat to the shore, and we jumped ashore. We looked around. There were lots of frightening things moving here and there. I threw the black clew there, and I threw the white clew behind myself. After that, I turned back and ran away. I followed the white clew as it rolled away. I ran all the way home. There were no sounds or voices of anything coming after me. I kept running after the white clew, and finally I was in front of my house. “Mother, I am back!” “Fine!” Saying so, my mother opened the door for us, and we went in. As there were no voices of anyone coming after me, we felt relieved. Then, as we had already grown up, I went to the mountains to hunt together with my younger brother. We killed deer and hares, and we fed our mother. We provided well for our mother. Finally, we even hunted large bears and were able to feed our mother well with good food. Eventually, our mother grew old and died. However, whenever I went to the mountains to hunt or did other things, I did everything together with my younger brother. I was always together with my younger brother. As I became an adult, I took a beautiful woman as my bride and married her. As for my brother, I also found him a beautiful woman as a bride. Whatever we did, we always did it together with my younger brother.
context: An Ainu folktale about two brothers, their mother, a dangerous uncle, and magical white and black clews used to escape danger.

title: Love Your Enemies
text: God teaches Christians to love their enemies and to show kindness to everyone. We should not only do good to people who are our friends, but also to people who may dislike us or treat us badly. In this story, a person chooses to help someone from another tribe, even though that tribe is hostile toward his own. Instead of responding with anger or hatred, he chooses to show compassion and do what is right. This teaches Christians that doing good should not depend on how another person treats us. Even when someone does something wrong to us, we should respond with kindness and forgiveness. God calls Christians to love others, including those who may consider them enemies.
context: A Christian teaching story about responding to hostility with kindness, compassion, forgiveness, and love.

title: The Laws
text: God gave Moses laws to guide his people and teach them how to live. These laws remind people to honor God and to treat others with respect. People should not worship idols or place other things above God. They should also set aside one day each week to rest from their work and honor Him. Children should respect and obey their parents. People must not kill, steal, or tell lies about others. They should also respect the marriages of others and remain faithful to their own spouses. God also teaches people not to desire what belongs to someone else. Instead of being jealous of another person's possessions or family, people should be grateful for what they have. These laws provide guidance for living faithfully, honestly, and peacefully with God and with other people.
context: A Christian teaching story about responding to hostility with kindness, compassion, forgiveness, and love.

title: The Prodigal Son
text: In this story, a young man has made many wrong choices. He takes the money his father gave him and spends it on a life of pleasure. Eventually, all of his money is gone, and the friends who were with him leave. The young man realizes what he has done and becomes sorry for his actions. He returns to his father and asks for forgiveness. His father welcomes him back because he loves him and forgives him. The story teaches that when we do wrong, we should recognize our mistakes, turn away from them, and ask for forgiveness. Christians are taught that Jesus loves people and offers forgiveness for their sins.
context: A Christian teaching story about repentance, forgiveness, and a father's unconditional love.

title: Emergence of the Myaamia
text: At first the Myaamia came out of the water. The place they emerged is called ‘Coming Out Place.’ The first ones emerged from the water. “Grab ahold of tree limbs”, they told each other. And they came out. Then they formed a town there. From there they went away. They left the town. After a while one returned. When he came back he saw the other people at Coming Out Place. To our surprise, their language was just like our language. They gave them a name. ‘Old Moccasins’ he called those people. I don’t know where they were from. Nobody knew where they went. This is how my mothers told me, my mother Seekaahkweeta, and her older sister Waapankihkwa. All the old Indian men believed it. They call the river ‘Coming Out River’ at the place where they came out from. Because of this people are named ‘Seekaahkweeta’, ‘Seekaahkonanka’, and ‘Seekaahkohkwa’.
context: A Myaamia traditional emergence story describing the people's origin from water, the Coming Out Place, their language, ancestors, and the coming Out River.
